medicines.name: Paracetamol
medicines.description: Paracetamol is thought to act mainly centrally, reducing prostaglandin synthesis via inhibition of cyclooxygenase pathways in the CNS, with a possible contribution from its metabolite AM404 acting on cannabinoid and TRPV1 systems. It has analgesic and antipyretic effects but minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory activity, and is a first-line agent for mild-to-moderate pain and fever.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults: 500-1000 mg orally every 4-6 hours as needed (minimum interval 4 hours). Maximum 4,000 mg in 24 hours from all sources; OTC labels for 500 mg tablets direct 2 tablets every 6 hours, not exceeding 6 tablets (3,000 mg) in 24 hours unless directed by a physician. Lower daily doses/longer intervals are used in severe renal impairment and hepatic impairment. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F).
medicines.black_box_warning: OTC oral labels carry a liver warning (severe liver damage with >4,000 mg/24 h, with other acetaminophen-containing products, or with 3 or more alcoholic drinks daily) rather than a boxed warning. Prescription and IV acetaminophen products carry a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity (acute liver failure, sometimes requiring transplant or fatal) and dosing errors.

Other acetaminophen-containing products (cold/flu combinations): risk of unintentional cumulative overdose.

medicines.name: Ibuprofen
medicines.description: Ibuprofen is a non-selective, reversible inhibitor of COX-1 and COX-2 that reduces prostaglandin synthesis, producing analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory effects. It is widely used for mild-to-moderate pain, fever, dysmenorrhea and inflammatory joint conditions.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults (OTC): 200-400 mg orally every 4-6 hours as needed, max 1,200 mg/day. Prescription: mild-to-moderate pain 400 mg every 4-6 hours as needed; rheumatoid arthritis/osteoarthritis 1,200-3,200 mg/day in divided doses. Take with food or milk; use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at room temperature; avoid excessive heat above 40 C (104 F).
medicines.black_box_warning: Cardiovascular risk: NSAIDs increase the risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction and stroke, which can be fatal; contraindicated for peri-operative pain in CABG surgery. Gastrointestinal risk: increased risk of serious GI bleeding, ulceration and perforation, which can be fatal and may occur without warning; older adults are at greater risk.

Methotrexate: increased methotrexate toxicity.

medicines.name: Mefenamic Acid
medicines.description: Mefenamic acid is an anthranilic acid (fenamate) NSAID that inhibits cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin synthesis. It is used for short-term relief of mild-to-moderate pain and for primary dysmenorrhea.

Primary dysmenorrhea: 500 mg initially, then 250 mg every 6 hours, starting with onset of bleeding and usually not needed beyond 2-3 days. Take with food. Refer to current product labeling.

medicines.name: Clopidogrel
medicines.description: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated mainly by CYP2C19 to a metabolite that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, preventing downstream glycoprotein IIb/IIIa activation and platelet aggregation. It is used, often with aspirin, in acute coronary syndromes and for secondary prevention after MI, stroke or peripheral arterial disease.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults: acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) 300 mg loading dose, then 75 mg once daily with aspirin; STEMI 75 mg once daily with or without a loading dose. Recent MI, recent stroke or established peripheral arterial disease: 75 mg once daily, with or without food. Discontinue 5 days before elective surgery when feasible. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 25 C (77 F); excursions permitted to 15-30 C (59-86 F).
medicines.black_box_warning: Diminished antiplatelet effect in patients with two loss-of-function CYP2C19 alleles (poor metabolizers), who have higher cardiovascular event rates at recommended doses; genetic testing is available, and an alternative P2Y12 inhibitor should be considered in identified poor metabolizers.

medicines.name: Warfarin
medicines.description: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), depleting reduced vitamin K and decreasing hepatic synthesis of functional clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S). It is used for prevention and treatment of venous thromboembolism and thromboembolism in atrial fibrillation and mechanical heart valves, with dosing guided by the INR.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults: usual initial dose 2-5 mg orally once daily, then individualized to the INR (target 2.0-3.0 for most indications, including VTE and atrial fibrillation; higher targets for some mechanical valves). Dose requirements vary with age, CYP2C9/VKORC1 genotype, diet and interacting drugs. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at controlled room temperature per the manufacturer's labeling.
medicines.black_box_warning: Bleeding risk: warfarin can cause major or fatal bleeding. Regular INR monitoring is required for all patients; drugs, dietary changes and other factors affect INR levels; patients should be instructed about bleeding prevention and to report signs and symptoms of bleeding.
medicines.source_attribution: FDA warfarin sodium label via DailyMed; StatPearls: Warfarin; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.

Hemorrhagic tendencies or blood dyscrasias

Vitamin K-rich foods: large changes in intake alter INR; botanicals (St John's wort, ginkgo, garlic) may alter effect.
Acetaminophen (regular high doses) and alcohol: may increase INR.

medicines.name: Amoxicillin
medicines.description: Amoxicillin is a bactericidal beta-lactam that binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits transpeptidation in bacterial cell-wall synthesis, leading to cell lysis. It is a first-line agent for many respiratory, ENT, skin and urinary infections and a component of H. pylori eradication regimens.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults: mild-to-moderate ENT, skin or genitourinary infection 500 mg every 12 hours or 250 mg every 8 hours; severe infections and lower respiratory tract infection 875 mg every 12 hours or 500 mg every 8 hours. H. pylori: 1 g twice daily with clarithromycin and a PPI (triple therapy) for 14 days. GFR 10-30 mL/min: 250-500 mg every 12 hours; GFR < 10: 250-500 mg every 24 hours; do not use the 875 mg dose if GFR < 30. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions permitted to 15-30 C (59-86 F).

medicines.description: Ciprofloxacin is a bactericidal fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication. medicines.name: Pyrazinamide
medicines.description: Pyrazinamide is a prodrug converted to pyrazinoic acid, which is active against semi-dormant M. tuberculosis in acidic environments; its exact mechanism is not fully understood. It is used during the 2-month intensive phase of first-line TB therapy, allowing total treatment to be shortened to 6 months.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults: 15-30 mg/kg orally once daily (maximum 2 g/day), or 50-75 mg/kg twice weekly based on lean body weight, always with other antituberculosis agents (typically for the first 2 months). Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at controlled room temperature 15-30 C (59-86 F) in a well-closed container.
medicines.source_attribution: FDA pyrazinamide tablet label via DailyMed; StatPearls: Antitubercular Medications; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.
indications: Active tuberculosis, intensive phase, in combination with other antituberculosis agents
adverse: Rash, photosensitivity; rare thrombocytopenia, dysuria, interstitial nephritis, porphyria exacerbation
contraindications: Severe hepatic damage
Hypersensitivity to pyrazinamide
Acute gout
interactions: Other hepatotoxic antituberculosis drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin): additive hepatotoxicity; monitor LFTs.
Uricosuric and anti-gout therapy (allopurinol, probenecid): pyrazinamide raises uric acid and may reduce their effect.

medicines.name: Ethambutol
medicines.description: Ethambutol inhibits mycobacterial arabinosyltransferases, interfering with arabinogalactan synthesis in the cell wall; it is bacteriostatic. It is included in the intensive phase of first-line TB therapy to protect against resistance while drug-susceptibility results are pending.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults: initial treatment 15 mg/kg orally once every 24 hours; retreatment 25 mg/kg once daily for 60 days, then 15 mg/kg once daily, always with other antituberculosis drugs. Dose reduction/extended interval (e.g., three times weekly when CrCl < 30 mL/min) is needed in renal impairment. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F).

medicines.name: Artemether + Lumefantrine
medicines.description: Artemether (and its metabolite dihydroartemisinin) rapidly reduces parasite biomass, while the long-acting lumefantrine eliminates residual parasites; both are thought to interfere with parasite heme detoxification and nucleic acid/protein synthesis. This fixed-dose artemisinin-based combination therapy is a WHO-recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults and patients >= 35 kg (20 mg/120 mg tablets): 4 tablets as an initial dose, 4 tablets again after 8 hours, then 4 tablets twice daily (morning and evening) for the following 2 days (total 6 doses, 24 tablets over 3 days). Take with food, ideally fat-containing, to enhance absorption; repeat the dose if vomiting occurs within 1-2 hours. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store at 25 C (77 F); excursions permitted to 15-30 C (59-86 F); dispense in a tight container.
medicines.source_attribution: FDA Coartem label via DailyMed; WHO malaria guidelines (Nov 2022 update, via MMV); Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.
indications: Acute uncomplicated malaria due to Plasmodium falciparum (including chloroquine-resistant strains)
Uncomplicated P. vivax malaria in areas where ACTs are used (per WHO guidance)
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to artemether, lumefantrine or excipients
Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort)
interactions: Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort): reduce artemether/lumefantrine exposure by up to about 70-90%; contraindicated.
CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, some antiretrovirals): increase exposure; monitor for QT effects.
QT-prolonging drugs (e.g., class IA/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones): additive QT risk; avoid halofantrine within 1 month.
Mefloquine given immediately before: reduced lumefantrine levels; ensure food intake.
Hormonal contraceptives: may be less effective; additional non-hormonal contraception advised.

medicines.name: Oseltamivir
medicines.description: Oseltamivir is an oral prodrug converted to oseltamivir carboxylate, a competitive inhibitor of influenza A and B neuraminidase that prevents release of new virions from infected cells. Started ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset, it shortens illness duration and is recommended for hospitalized and high-risk patients; it is also used for post-exposure prophylaxis.
medicines.dosage_text: Adults and adolescents >= 13 years: treatment 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days (begin within 48 hours of symptom onset); prophylaxis 75 mg once daily for at least 10 days after exposure (up to 6 weeks during a community outbreak). Renal adjustment: CrCl > 30-60 mL/min 30 mg twice daily (treatment); CrCl > 10-30 mL/min 30 mg once daily (treatment); hemodialysis 30 mg after each dialysis cycle. Refer to current product labeling.
medicines.storage: Store capsules at 25 C (77 F); excursions permitted to 15-30 C (59-86 F).
medicines.source_attribution: FDA Tamiflu label via DailyMed; StatPearls: Oseltamivir; Goodman & Gilman's 14th ed.
indications: Treatment of acute uncomplicated influenza A and B in patients symptomatic for no more than 48 hours
Prophylaxis of influenza A and B
adverse: Neuropsychiatric events (delirium, abnormal behavior), mainly reported in children
Serious skin/hypersensitivity reactions: anaphylaxis, SJS, TEN, erythema multiforme
contraindications: Known serious hypersensitivity to oseltamivir or any component of the product
interactions: Live attenuated influenza vaccine (intranasal): avoid within 2 weeks before or 48 hours after oseltamivir (antiviral may reduce vaccine efficacy); inactivated vaccine is not affected.
Clopidogrel: in vitro inhibition of oseltamivir activation (carboxylesterase 1) has been described; clinical significance uncertain.
